e.etymology: From Greek asterios, starry, from aster, star. In Greek myth Asteria is a Titan goddess of falling stars and the mother of Hecate.
From French Michèle, a spelling of Michelle, the feminine of Michael, from Hebrew for who is like God? In Italian, Michele, said mee-KEH-leh, is the men's form of Michael.
A spelling of Janet or Jeanette, pet forms of Jane and French Jeanne, the feminine of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.

A name of uncertain and probably mixed origin. Spanish and Portuguese Élida is the name of Elis, the region of ancient Greece that held the Olympic Games; in Norway Ellida is known from Ibsen's play The Lady from the Sea.
A modern name in the family of Anissa and Vanessa. It can be read as Anissa respelled or as Vanessa without the V; it has no settled meaning.
The Polish, Hungarian and German spelling of Bianca, the Italian word for white and the counterpart of French Blanche.
A modern American name said like Monet, the surname of French painter Claude Monet, with the -ae ending of Janae and Renae.
namesakes: Janelle Monae (singer and actress; a surname)

e.etymology: A respelling of Malia or Maleah using the -leigh of Ashleigh. Malia is the Hawaiian form of Mary.
An English surname for someone who worked for an abbot, the head of a monastery. Abbot goes back through Latin and Greek to Aramaic abba, father.

assoc.t: Abbott and Costello, the classic comedy duo
Abbott, the health care and medical device company

e.etymology: A respelling of Leah or Leia. Leah is the Biblical wife of Jacob; the Hebrew name is traditionally glossed as weary, though its origin is debated.
The name of Ix Chel, the Maya goddess of the moon, childbirth, medicine and weaving. In Yucatec Maya it is usually read as Lady Rainbow.
e.note: The x is said sh, as eesh-CHEL; most Americans will need the pronunciation explained.

e.etymology: A modern American name that extends Amari and Amara with the -iyah of Aaliyah. It matches Amariah, a Biblical men's name from Hebrew, the Lord has said.
The Ethiopian and Hebrew form of Jared, from Hebrew yered, descent. Saint Yared was the 6th-century Ethiopian composer credited with founding the church's sacred music.
A modern American coinage that blends Aniya and Nyla. It has no meaning of its own.
The Portuguese and Italian form of Gaius, one of the most common Roman first names, as in Gaius Julius Caesar. Its original meaning is unknown. It is especially popular in Brazil.

e.meaning: sweet as honey; a name of Krishna
e.etymology: From Sanskrit Madhava, a derivative of madhu, honey or sweetness. It is one of the best-known names of Krishna and Vishnu.
A modern Indian name, made familiar by actress Avika Gor. Name books give meanings such as sun rays or the earth, but its derivation is not well documented.
From Nahuatl quetzalli, the brilliant green tail feather of the quetzal bird and, by extension, something precious. It is used in Mexican and Mexican American families.
A respelling of Waylon, itself a form of Wayland, the master smith of Germanic legend. Country singer Waylon Jennings made the name familiar in the US.
A spelling of Lyla or Lila, names tied to Arabic layla, night, and Sanskrit lila, play. This spelling is that of Lylla, the otter in Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 (2023).
A respelling of Alaia. Alaia is linked to Basque alai, joyful, and is also the surname of designer Azzedine Alaia, whose Paris fashion house carries the name.
A compound of Anna and Leia, in the family of Annalise and Analia. It has no separate meaning.
A modern coinage from French ciel, sky or heaven, given the -elle ending of Brielle and Noelle. It is not a traditional French name.
A modern American coinage in the style of Zyaire and Nasir. It has no established meaning.
From Sanskrit vayu, wind or air. Vayu is the Hindu god of the wind and the father of Hanuman and Bhima.
A respelling of Jersey, the name of the Channel Island and, by way of New Jersey, an American place name; jersey is also the word for a knit sports shirt.
A Norman surname from places in France called Chancé. It became an American first name in honor of Charles Chauncy, an early president of Harvard.
namesakes: Chauncey Billups (NBA champion guard and coach)

e.etymology: The Italian and Spanish word for saint or holy, from Latin sanctus. As a first name it is mostly Italian.
The short form of Gabriel, from Hebrew Gavriel, God is my strength, the archangel who announces the births of John the Baptist and Jesus.
namesakes: Gabe Kaplan (comedian and star of Welcome Back, Kotter)

e.etymology: A surname, a variant of Crichton, from a place in Midlothian, Scotland, whose name joins Gaelic crioch, border, and Old English tun, settlement.

assoc.t: Creighton University in Omaha and its Bluejays

e.etymology: Jordan with a feminine -a. Jordan is the river of the Holy Land, from Hebrew Yarden, from a root meaning to descend or flow down.
namesakes: Jordana Brewster (actress, the Fast and Furious films)

e.etymology: A spelling of Wynn, from Welsh gwyn, white, fair or blessed. As an English surname it can also come from Old English wine, friend.
